chapters.title: Chapter 5: Valuation and Fundamental Mean Reversion

lessons.title: P/E Reversion: Do Expensive Stocks Really Get Cheap Again?

children.text: Everything so far in this course has worked on a timescale of days to weeks: a price stretched from its 20-day average, an RSI reading, a VIX spike around a dated event. Valuation multiples move on a much slower clock, quarters to years, but the underlying question is identical to the one this course opened with. A stock's P/E ratio at 32, against its own five-year average of 22, is the exact same kind of statement as a price sitting three standard deviations below its 20-day mean. Something has moved unusually far from where it normally sits. The only new question this chapter adds is what actually needs to happen for it to close.

body.text: A P/E ratio can revert to its historical average in two completely different ways: the price can fall, or earnings can grow to catch up with the price. Both close the same statistical gap. Only one of them feels like a loss to a shareholder who is already holding the stock.

children.text: Applying the Same Z-Score to a New Variable

body.caption: Exactly Lesson 5's z-score formula, with a trailing average P/E and its standard deviation, usually computed over 5 to 10 years of quarterly or annual data, replacing the 20-day rolling window used for price.

children.text: Take a stock with a five-year average P/E of 22 and a standard deviation of 4, currently trading at a P/E of 32. Its valuation z-score is (32 minus 22) divided by 4, which is 2.5, comfortably past the same plus-2 threshold Lesson 5 flagged as statistically notable. Every caution from Chapter 1 applies here without modification. A high valuation z-score tells you the multiple is unusual. It says nothing about whether that is a temporary premium waiting to compress or a permanent re-rating that is here to stay.
Two Ways a Stretched P/E Can Close

body.caption: Price falling and earnings catching up both compress a P/E, but they are not the same experience for a shareholder

cells: Can stay flat, or keep rising, just more slowly than earnings
Grows into the price over subsequent quarters
A real loss if bought near the peak multiple
No loss at all, and often continued gains
Sentiment-driven premium with no earnings support behind it
A genuinely strong growth story that the market priced in slightly ahead of schedule

body.text: This is why a high valuation z-score alone is a weak short or sell signal. Titan Company and Asian Paints, the long-term compounders from Lesson 2, have traded at price-to-earnings multiples well above the broader market's average for most of the last two decades, and largely stayed there, because their earnings kept growing fast enough to keep justifying the premium. Their P/E never had to compress the hard way, because the business kept closing the gap from the other side.

children.text: Lesson 3's three reasons a series fails to be stationary map directly onto valuation multiples. A stock can be structurally growing into a durably higher multiple, exactly the Titan and Asian Paints case, in which case the old, lower average P/E is simply outdated history, not a level to expect a return to. A stock can be structurally declining toward a durably lower multiple, if the market has correctly identified a permanent deterioration in growth or returns on capital, in which case a 'cheap relative to its own history' P/E is not a bargain. Or a stock can experience a one-time re-rating, a specific catalyst, a change in promoter holding, an index inclusion, a genuine strategic pivot, that permanently shifts its fair multiple to a new, different, but still stable level. In all three cases, the old average P/E is the wrong number to expect a reversion toward. Only a temporary, sentiment-driven premium or discount, with no underlying change in the business, is a genuine mean reversion candidate.

body.title: A mean-reverting P/E vs a structurally re-rated P/E, over 20 quarters (illustrative)

body.code:
import pandas as pd

# 'pe_ratio' is a pandas Series of quarterly P/E readings
window = 20  # 20 quarters = 5 years, not 20 trading days

rolling_mean = pe_ratio.rolling(window).mean()
rolling_std = pe_ratio.rolling(window).std()

pe_zscore = (pe_ratio - rolling_mean) / rolling_std

print(pe_zscore.tail())
body.caption: The identical rolling z-score calculation from Lesson 5, applied to quarterly P/E data instead of daily prices. Note the window is now measured in quarters, not trading days.

body.title: Compute a valuation z-score
body.prompt: A stock's 5-year average P/E is 18, with a standard deviation of 3. It currently trades at a P/E of 24. What is its valuation z-score?
body.explanation: (24 - 18) / 3 = 6 / 3 = 2.0. A z-score of 2 clears the common statistical threshold from Lesson 5, but on its own says nothing about whether this is a temporary premium or the start of a durable re-rating.

body.title: Which stretched P/E is the better reversion candidate?
body.question: Stock X and Stock Y are both trading at a P/E of 35, against a five-year average of 20 for each. Stock X has just signed multi-year contracts that have led analysts to durably raise their long-term earnings growth estimates across the board. Stock Y's P/E has risen on retail trading enthusiasm alone, with no change to analyst earnings estimates or the underlying business. Which stock's P/E is the better mean-reversion candidate for compression back toward its old average?
options: Stock X, because a higher P/E always eventually reverts regardless of the reason behind it
Stock Y, because its premium has no earnings support and no fundamental change behind it
Both are equally good candidates since their P/E and historical average are identical
Neither, because P/E ratios never actually revert in real markets
body.explanation: Stock X's premium is backed by a durable, analyst-confirmed change in its earnings outlook, the re-rating case from this lesson, where the old average P/E is likely outdated rather than a target to revert to. Stock Y's premium has no such support, making it a genuine candidate for compression back toward its historical average, either through price falling or, less likely here given the lack of earnings support, through earnings catching up.

cards.definition: A stock's current P/E (or other multiple) minus its own historical average, divided by the historical standard deviation, the same z-score formula from Lesson 5 applied to valuation instead of price.
A P/E ratio falling back toward its historical average, which can happen either through the price falling or through earnings growing to catch up with an unchanged or rising price.

A durable, structural shift in a stock's fair valuation multiple to a new, different, but still stable level, driven by a genuine change in its growth prospects, capital structure, or strategic position.

points: The same z-score formula from Chapter 2 applies directly to valuation multiples, just computed over quarters or years of data instead of trading days.
A stretched P/E can close in two different ways: price falling (a real loss for existing shareholders) or earnings growing into the price (no loss, and often continued gains).

Chapter 1's three reasons a series fails to be stationary, structural growth, structural decline, and one-time re-rating, apply directly to valuation multiples. Only a temporary, sentiment-driven premium with no fundamental support is a genuine reversion candidate.

Long-term compounders like Titan and Asian Paints have sustained above-market P/E multiples for years without reverting, because durable earnings growth kept closing the gap from the earnings side rather than the price side.
Lesson 2 next applies this same logic at the sector level, and Lesson 3 closes the chapter with a real, multi-year case study on Indian PSU banks.
